notes: NIST AI RMF is mapped at function and category level. Subcategory-level mapping is a v1.0 target.
Every mapping carries a role scope naming who the obligation falls on. Mappings without a role scope do not publish.
Regulatory mappings are research aids and do not constitute legal advice or establish compliance.
Plain-language examples are composites written for recognition, not descriptions of any specific organization.

failureModes.name: No executive-approved AI policy
failureModes.plainTerms: Nobody has written down what the company will and won't do with AI. Every team decides for itself, and no two teams decide the same way.

failureModes.name: Policy not mapped to operations
failureModes.plainTerms: There's a twelve-page AI policy. It lives in a shared drive. Nobody's day-to-day work changed when it was published.

failureModes.name: No risk-tier taxonomy
failureModes.plainTerms: Every AI project is treated the same. A tool that suggests lunch spots gets the same scrutiny as one that declines loan applications.

failureModes.name: Prohibited-use categories unenforced
failureModes.plainTerms: The policy says the company will never use AI for a particular purpose. Nothing in any system actually prevents someone from doing it.

failureModes.name: No accountable executive owner
failureModes.plainTerms: Ask who owns AI risk and you get four names, a committee, and a shrug.

failureModes.name: Policy unversioned / no change control
failureModes.plainTerms: Someone edited the AI policy in March. Nobody can say what it said in February, or who changed it, or why.

failureModes.name: Strategy–execution disconnect
failureModes.plainTerms: Leadership announced an AI strategy. The projects actually being funded have very little to do with it.

failureModes.name: No value measurement for the AI programme
failureModes.plainTerms: The AI programme has been running eighteen months. When the CFO asks what it delivered, the answer is a list of projects, not a number — so at the next budget cycle, governance reads as pure cost.

failureModes.name: Intake bypass
failureModes.plainTerms: A team bought an AI tool on a corporate card, rolled it out to forty people, and the governance team found out when someone mentioned it in an unrelated meeting.
failureModes.description: A use case reaches production without ever entering the governance intake process. It is never tiered, never reviewed, and never approved — so no downstream control in the lifecycle can attach to it.
variants: .01 Procurement path — AI purchased as software and never flagged as AI
.02 Embedded-SaaS path — AI features switched on inside an already-approved vendor tool
.04 Individually adopted tooling brought into a team workflow
failureModes.sectors: Cross-sector
indicators: AI expenditure appearing with no corresponding intake record
SaaS AI features enabled without a change request
Model or API traffic originating from teams with no registered use case
Vendor renewal documentation describing capabilities absent from the register
rootCauses: Intake operates as a request rather than a gate, so nothing structurally prevents bypass
Procurement and governance workflows are not integrated
Intake is perceived as slow, so delivery teams route around it — see AGF-F027 and AGF-F037
mitigations: Integrate procurement with governance so AI expenditure triggers intake automatically
Scan for AI features newly enabled within the existing SaaS estate
Make the gate structural by tying it to funding release or access provisioning
Run amnesty-based discovery drives that surface existing bypasses without penalty
Address review throughput first — enforcement without a fast path drives bypass underground

failureModes.reference: No single canonical public incident. Prevalence is supported by Verizon DBIR 2026 and IBM/Ponemon 2025 findings on unauthorized AI use.

failureModes.name: Unsanctioned AI use
failureModes.plainTerms: Half the department is pasting work into a free chatbot on their phones. It isn't on any list, because nobody ever decided to use it — people just started.
failureModes.description: Individuals use unsanctioned AI tools on corporate data and devices, entirely outside any governance perimeter. Distinct from intake bypass in that no organizational adoption decision occurs at all — adoption is individual and invisible.
failureModes.sectors: Cross-sector; consequences most acute in banking, biopharma, and insurance where the underlying data is regulated
indicators: Personal-account access to AI services from corporate devices
Cloud access security telemetry showing traffic to consumer AI domains
Expense claims for individual AI subscriptions
Sensitive document volume moving toward consumer AI endpoints
rootCauses: Sanctioned tooling is slower, less capable, or unavailable for the task
No approved-tool catalog exists, so there is nothing concrete to comply with
An enforcement-only posture drives usage further underground rather than eliminating it
Pent-up demand created by slow or opaque approval — see AGF-F037
mitigations: Provide fast sanctioned pathways rather than relying on prohibition alone
Apply redaction and data-loss controls at the egress point
Publish an approved-tool catalog with a genuinely fast addition process
Lead with amnesty-based discovery before enforcement

mapping.provision: Art. 4 — AI literacy obligation, in force since 2 Feb 2025. The clearest currently-enforceable hook for ungoverned staff use.
Art. 50 — where unsanctioned output reaches customers, the disclosure duty still attaches
GOVERN-1, MAP-1 — inventory and context
Clause 4.1 context; A.2 policies related to AI; A.9 use of AI systems
Inventory and scope determination

failureModes.reference: Widely reported corporate source-code exposure through consumer AI assistants (2023) led to internal prohibitions at several large manufacturers. Netskope 2026 reports 47% of generative AI users on personal, unmanaged accounts.

failureModes.name: Incomplete intake — context, data or owner missing
failureModes.plainTerms: The intake form was submitted with 'TBD' for data sources and 'various' for the owner. It was approved anyway, because sending it back would have taken another three weeks.

failureModes.name: No continuous or adaptive intake
failureModes.plainTerms: Intake happens once a quarter in a big batch. Anything that comes up in between either waits three months or quietly skips the process.

failureModes.name: Duplicate use cases undetected
failureModes.plainTerms: Three teams built three versions of the same document summarizer. None of them knew about the others. All three went through review separately.

failureModes.name: Vendor-supplied AI uncaptured in inventory
failureModes.plainTerms: The HR system the company has used for years quietly added AI-driven candidate ranking in an update. It's now an AI system, but it's still filed as an HR system.

failureModes.name: Agentic components not distinguished from models
failureModes.plainTerms: The register says 'AI assistant.' It's actually an agent that can send emails and update records on its own — which is a completely different risk, recorded as if it were the same one.

failureModes.name: Fragmented intake surfaces
failureModes.plainTerms: Submitting an idea means filling out four different forms owned by four different teams, with most of the questions repeated across all of them. Most people fill out one and stop.

failureModes.name: No triage or routing layer
failureModes.plainTerms: An idea gets submitted, sits with the wrong team for two weeks, is forwarded to a second team, who forward it to a third. Nobody rejected it. It just circulated until the submitter gave up.
failureModes.description: Submissions enter the organization with no upfront triage step that determines where they belong. Items route by guesswork, bounce between functions, and accumulate delay that is invisible in any single team's metrics because no single team ever held the item long enough to own the wait.
failureModes.sectors: Cross-sector; worst where innovation, operational excellence, and AI governance run as separate intake channels
indicators: Submissions with multiple reassignments before first substantive review
Elapsed time far exceeding the sum of active review time
Submitters re-submitting the same idea through a different channel
No single queue where all incoming requests are visible
rootCauses: Multiple teams each built their own intake channel independently
No agreed criteria for which path a submission belongs on
Routing is a judgement call made by whoever receives the item first
Nobody owns the end-to-end submitter experience
mitigations: Establish a single upfront triage step preceding all routing decisions
Publish explicit routing criteria so classification is repeatable rather than discretionary
Make the full queue visible across functions so bouncing is observable
Measure and report elapsed time from submission, not active time per team
Assign ownership of the submission experience to a named role

mapping.provision: GOVERN-2 — accountability structures and role clarity
Clause 5.3 — organizational roles, responsibilities and authorities
Governance and accountability expectations
Process-design failure with no specific statutory hook. Mapped for completeness, not compliance.

failureModes.reference: Manifests as submitter attrition and shadow adoption rather than as a reportable incident.

failureModes.name: No consistent scoring methodology
failureModes.plainTerms: Two reviewers assess similar projects and reach different conclusions, because the scoring criteria exist in their heads rather than on paper.

failureModes.name: Tier assigned once, never revisited
failureModes.plainTerms: A tool was rated low risk when it drafted internal emails. It now drafts customer communications. It is still rated low risk.

failureModes.name: Miscategorization — high-impact rated low
failureModes.plainTerms: A system that influences who gets hired was filed as a productivity tool, because it doesn't make the final call — a person does, after reading its ranking.

failureModes.name: Transparency-triggering uses not flagged
failureModes.plainTerms: Customers are chatting with an AI agent and nobody told them. Nothing in the assessment ever asked whether they would need to be told.
failureModes.description: Use cases that trigger a legal duty to disclose AI involvement to an end user are not identified as such during assessment, so the disclosure obligation is never implemented anywhere downstream. Art. 50 applies by system function rather than risk tier, so the Annex III deferral provides no relief here.
failureModes.sectors: Cross-sector; acute for organizations with EU-facing customers or operations
indicators: Customer-facing AI outputs carrying no disclosure language
No transparency-trigger field on the risk assessment form
AI-generated service or marketing content published without labelling
No record of which use cases touch EU data subjects
rootCauses: The assessment framework predates the transparency obligations and was never revised
Transparency treated as a legal question rather than an assessment field
Assumption that an internal-only classification excludes disclosure duties
Assumption that the high-risk deferral moved Art. 50 as well — it did not
mitigations: Add an explicit transparency-trigger question to the assessment form
Maintain a disclosure register mapped to individual use cases
Automate machine-readable marking where synthetic content is generated
Re-screen the existing portfolio rather than only new intake

failureModes.reference: Art. 50 became enforceable 2 Aug 2026. Applies by system function, not risk tier, so mainstream generative deployments are in scope regardless of the Annex III deferral to Dec 2027.

failureModes.name: No regulatory trigger built into assessment
failureModes.plainTerms: The assessment asks thorough questions about data and security. It never asks which laws apply, so nobody finds out until someone in legal reads about it in the news.

failureModes.name: Aggregate portfolio risk unassessed
failureModes.plainTerms: Every individual AI project is low risk. Nobody has asked what it means that forty of them now depend on the same vendor's model.

failureModes.name: Bias and fairness risk unassessed
failureModes.plainTerms: A screening tool has been running for two years. Nobody has ever checked whether it treats different groups of applicants the same way.

failureModes.name: Undifferentiated review burden
failureModes.plainTerms: Every AI request — including one to summarize meeting notes — goes through the full security, architecture, privacy and legal review. It takes eleven weeks, the reviewers are drowning, and teams have quietly stopped asking.
failureModes.description: Governance applies the same depth of review to every use case regardless of risk. The result is not more safety: reviewer capacity is consumed by low-risk items, genuinely high-risk items receive no additional attention because there is none left to give, and the delay drives teams out of the process entirely.
failureModes.sectors: Cross-sector; most acute in regulated industries where review functions are already at capacity
indicators: Identical review path and duration across trivially and materially different use cases
Specialist review functions reporting sustained backlog
Review cycle times measured in months
Rising proportion of use cases discovered after deployment rather than at intake
Reviewers approving late-stage items without substantive examination in order to clear queue
rootCauses: Risk tiering was never established, or exists on paper without routing consequences — see AGF-F003
Caution is expressed by adding reviewers rather than by directing them
No mechanism exists to route by risk, so the only safe default is to route everything everywhere
Fear that a fast path will be blamed if something goes wrong
mitigations: Establish tiered intake where low-risk use cases follow a materially shorter path
Route by questionnaire trigger so only the relevant specialist functions are engaged
Require attestation to core controls on the fast path, with sampled post-hoc validation
Measure reviewer load and cycle time per tier, and publish both
Treat sustained backlog as a governance failure in its own right rather than a resourcing complaint

mapping.provision: Materiality-proportionate validation — the 2026 guidance explicitly moves toward tailoring and risk-based scaling, making undifferentiated review a departure from current supervisory expectation rather than a conservative reading of it
Art. 9 — risk management system proportionate to risk
MAP-1, MANAGE-1 — risk prioritization and resource allocation
Clause 6.1 — actions to address risks and opportunities, proportionate to impact

failureModes.reference: Presents as reviewer burnout and shadow adoption. Rarely reported as an incident, because the failure is the absence of governance rather than its malfunction.

failureModes.name: Unauthorized or unqualified approver
failureModes.plainTerms: The approval was signed by whoever was available that week, not by anyone with the authority or the background to judge it.

failureModes.name: Stale approval
failureModes.plainTerms: The system was approved two years ago. The vendor has swapped the underlying model twice since then. The record still says 'approved,' and technically it is.
failureModes.description: A use case continues to operate under an approval that has been invalidated by a subsequent change — to the model, the vendor, the data, or the applicable regulation — because no re-review was triggered.
variants: .01 Following a model change — the underlying model was replaced or retrained
.02 Following a regulatory change — the rule the approval relied upon has moved
failureModes.sectors: Cross-sector; consequences highest in banking and biopharma
indicators: Approval dates materially older than the last model or vendor change
Approval records with no expiry
Regulatory change logs with no linked re-review activity
Vendor release notes with no corresponding governance event
rootCauses: Approvals modelled as one-time events rather than time-boxed states
No structural linkage between change management and the approval record
No owner monitoring regulatory change against the existing portfolio
mitigations: Time-box every approval with a defined expiry
Trigger re-review on model, vendor, data, or regulatory change
Link change records to approval records structurally rather than by convention
Operate a regulatory-change-to-portfolio impact process

mapping.provision: Art. 72 — post-market monitoring system, running across the operational lifetime. Corrected in v0.3 from Art. 61, cited in error in earlier versions.
Art. 9 — risk management as a continuous iterative process, not a one-time assessment
MANAGE-2, GOVERN-1 — ongoing management and policy currency
Clause 9 performance evaluation; Clause 10 improvement
Ongoing monitoring and periodic review
Periodic review requirements

failureModes.reference: Typically surfaced during examination or inspection rather than as a publicly reported incident.

failureModes.name: Use outside approved scope
failureModes.plainTerms: A tool approved to draft internal summaries is now generating content that goes to customers. No new approval was sought, because to everyone involved it felt like the same tool doing the same thing.
failureModes.description: A system approved for one narrow purpose is progressively used for others. Each extension appears minor in isolation; the cumulative result is a system operating well outside its assessed and approved risk profile.
failureModes.sectors: Manufacturing, insurance, banking, professional services
indicators: Usage patterns diverging from the documented intended-use statement
New user groups onboarded with no corresponding governance event
Output types appearing that were absent from the original assessment
Vendor capability expansion adopted without re-intake
rootCauses: No documented use-case boundary statement exists to be breached
Success in the approved use invites informal extension
Nothing monitors actual usage against approved scope
mitigations: Require an explicit use-case boundary statement at the point of approval
Monitor usage against declared boundaries
Define re-intake triggers for scope extension
Treat vendor capability changes as a governance event

mapping.provision: Art. 26 — deployers must use the system in accordance with the provider's instructions for use. Use outside intended purpose is the clearest deployer-side breach in the Act.
Art. 50 — a scope extension into customer-facing output activates transparency duties immediately, independent of the high-risk deferral
Art. 25 — a deployer who substantially modifies purpose may itself become a provider
MAP-1, MANAGE-1 — intended purpose and context
A.9 — responsible use of AI systems; Clause 8 operational control

Use consistent with validation scope

failureModes.reference: Commonly identified during internal audit rather than through public incident reporting.

failureModes.name: Conditional-approval conditions never verified
failureModes.plainTerms: Approval was granted on condition the team added human review and logging before launch. They launched. Nobody ever checked whether they added either.

failureModes.name: No defined responsibility model for approval
failureModes.plainTerms: Four people have to sign off. None of them can say which parts they are each responsible for, so each waits to see what the others do first.

failureModes.name: Approval without substantive review
failureModes.plainTerms: The committee approves everything. Nobody can recall the last time a request was sent back with a material objection.

failureModes.name: Emergency approval with no subsequent review
failureModes.plainTerms: Something urgent got approved in a hallway conversation to hit a deadline. The proper review was going to happen right after launch. That was a year ago.

failureModes.name: No service level on review decisions
failureModes.plainTerms: Teams submit a request and hear nothing for six weeks. There's no published turnaround time, so nothing is ever technically late — and people stop waiting and start improvising.
failureModes.description: No committed turnaround exists for governance decisions. Because nothing is late by definition, delay is never escalated, never measured, and never treated as a defect. The predictable consequence is that teams route around governance rather than wait for it.
failureModes.sectors: Cross-sector
indicators: No published turnaround commitment for any review stage
Submitters contacting reviewers directly to ask about status
Items with no status change for extended periods and no escalation triggered
Pent-up demand visible as a surge whenever a fast path is announced
Rising discovery of deployed systems that never entered review
rootCauses: Governance designed around thoroughness with no throughput commitment
No owner of end-to-end cycle time
Escalation paths defined for risk but not for delay
Capacity constraints treated as immovable rather than as a governable parameter
mitigations: Publish service levels per review tier and report performance against them
Trigger automatic escalation when an item exceeds its service level
Operate a regular triage cadence rather than ad-hoc scheduling
Make cycle time a reported governance metric alongside risk metrics
Treat sustained service-level breach as a finding, not as background noise

mapping.provision: GOVERN-2, GOVERN-4 — accountability structures and organizational practice
Clause 5.3 roles and authorities; Clause 9.1 monitoring and measurement
Governance and accountability expectations
No instrument mandates a governance service level. The regulatory consequence is indirect: latency causes the bypass and unsanctioned-use failures that do carry obligations.

failureModes.reference: Presents as shadow adoption and submitter attrition rather than as a reportable incident. The causal link between review latency and unsanctioned use is the most consistent pattern in this catalog.

failureModes.name: No precedent reuse
failureModes.plainTerms: The same question — can we use this kind of model with this kind of data — has now been answered eight times by eight different reviewers. There's no record of the previous answers, so the ninth team starts from scratch.
failureModes.description: Each review is conducted from first principles because prior decisions are not captured in reusable form. Reviewer effort is spent re-deriving conclusions that already exist, decisions drift as different reviewers reach different answers to the same question, and the organization cannot demonstrate consistency of treatment.
failureModes.sectors: Cross-sector; compounding cost rises with portfolio size
indicators: Reviewers unable to cite a prior decision on a materially identical question
Similar use cases receiving different conditions or outcomes
No searchable repository of past decisions, guidance, or accepted patterns
Review duration not decreasing as volume increases
rootCauses: Decisions recorded as approvals rather than as reasoning
No repository for guidance, patterns, or reference architectures
Review treated as a per-item task rather than as an accumulating knowledge base
Reviewer turnover with no capture of accumulated judgement
mitigations: Maintain a searchable repository of decisions, guidance, and accepted patterns
Record the reasoning, not only the outcome
Define pre-approved patterns that qualifying use cases can adopt without full review
Publish playbooks for recurring use-case archetypes
Measure the proportion of reviews resolved by precedent as a programme health metric

mapping.provision: GOVERN-1, GOVERN-4 — policy, process and organizational knowledge
Clause 7.5 — documented information
Documentation expectations supporting consistent treatment

failureModes.reference: Presents as persistent reviewer load and inconsistent treatment of comparable cases.

failureModes.name: Review sequencing mismatch
failureModes.plainTerms: Review step three requires test results that only get produced at step five. Every request reaches step three, gets sent back, and goes around again. Everyone involved knows. Nobody has changed the order.
failureModes.description: Governance gates are ordered so that an earlier stage requires artifacts produced by a later one. Items cycle repeatedly between stages, consuming reviewer capacity and elapsed time without adding assurance. The failure is structural: no amount of additional effort or resourcing resolves it, because the loop is built into the sequence.
failureModes.sectors: Cross-sector; most visible in organizations with formal multi-stage review
indicators: Items repeatedly transitioning backward between the same two stages
Reviewers routinely rejecting for missing artifacts rather than for substance
Average number of stage transitions materially exceeding the number of stages
Teams pre-emptively producing artifacts out of sequence to avoid the loop
Stage-level metrics that look healthy while end-to-end cycle time does not
rootCauses: Stages designed independently by the functions that own them
No end-to-end process owner with authority to reorder gates
Artifact dependencies never mapped against stage sequence
Loop normalized over time and re-described as 'how the process works'
mitigations: Map artifact dependencies against stage order and reorder where they conflict
Introduce an explicit stage for producing prerequisite artifacts before the gate requiring them
Assign end-to-end process ownership with authority to change sequencing
Instrument backward transitions as a first-class metric
Review process design when backward transition rates exceed a defined threshold

mapping.provision: Art. 17 — quality management system covering the design and sequence of control processes. EN 18286:2026 is the supporting harmonized standard.
GOVERN-2, MANAGE-1 — process design and accountability
Clause 8.1 — operational planning and control

failureModes.reference: Widely experienced, rarely documented — the loop is usually described as a resourcing problem rather than a design defect.

failureModes.name: Missing human-in-the-loop trigger
failureModes.plainTerms: The policy says a person reviews every high-value decision. In the actual system, there is no screen where a person could do that, and no record that anyone ever has.
failureModes.description: A decision pathway that requires human review under policy or law has no mechanism that enforces the review. The system decides and acts autonomously in cases where a human was supposed to intervene.
failureModes.sectors: Banking (credit, fraud), insurance (claims), employment screening, healthcare
indicators: Decision logs containing no human-review event
Automated approval rates at or near 100%
No reviewer identity captured on high-impact decisions
Review queue depth of zero on a pathway that should be generating reviews
rootCauses: Human oversight specified in policy prose but never implemented as a system control
Review thresholds defined qualitatively and therefore unenforceable
Volume pressure leads to the checkpoint being disabled without a governance decision
mitigations: Define review thresholds numerically and enforce them in the system
Make the checkpoint blocking rather than advisory
Run sampling audits of automated decisions to confirm the pathway operates
Capture and retain reviewer identity as evidence

failureModes.reference: A recurring contributing factor across publicly reported automated-decision harms in the AI Incident Database.

failureModes.name: Human review present but not substantive
failureModes.plainTerms: There is a review step. The reviewer processes four hundred items an hour. It is a button, not a judgement.

failureModes.name: Orphaned ownership
failureModes.plainTerms: The person who built and owned the system left in March. The system is still running, still making decisions, and has no owner.

failureModes.name: No escalation path
failureModes.plainTerms: Someone on the front line notices the AI is producing something wrong. There is no route for that concern to go anywhere, so they work around it and tell a colleague.

failureModes.name: Diffused accountability across functions
failureModes.plainTerms: A decision needs risk, legal, data, and the business to agree. Getting them in the same room takes three weeks. The decision itself takes ten minutes.
failureModes.description: Responsibility is spread across business, data, technology, legal, and risk functions with no single owner. Reviews stall in handoffs, decisions require assembling people who do not report to one another, and when something fails nobody is accountable because everybody was involved.
failureModes.sectors: Cross-sector; most pronounced in large matrixed organizations
indicators: Long elapsed time against short active working time on governance reviews
Use cases stalling between functions rather than within them
No named owner recorded on a material proportion of the register
Escalations resolved by seniority rather than by defined authority
rootCauses: Governance designed as a committee rather than as a process
No responsibility model, or one that exists on paper only
Each function optimizes its own step while nobody owns end-to-end cycle time
mitigations: Publish a responsibility model with named accountable roles at each stage
Operate a single orchestration workspace so handoffs are visible
Set per-stage service levels with escalation on breach
Measure and report end-to-end cycle time rather than per-step throughput

failureModes.reference: Manifests as slow delivery and unattributable failure rather than as a discrete incident.

failureModes.name: No override or appeal route for affected individuals
failureModes.plainTerms: A customer was declined by an automated decision. There is no way for them to ask a human to look at it again, and no one inside the company who could act if they did.

failureModes.name: Governance owner without capacity
failureModes.plainTerms: One person owns AI governance. It is not their only job, or their second. They are in meetings all day, and the governance work happens on weekends — or it doesn't.

failureModes.name: Process communication diverges from routing logic
failureModes.plainTerms: The screen tells the submitter their request is going to expert review. The rules actually send it somewhere else entirely. Nobody notices until someone goes looking for a review that never happened.

failureModes.name: Undocumented data lineage
failureModes.plainTerms: Ask where the training data came from and the answer is the name of a person who might remember.

failureModes.name: Data-use rights and consent unverified
failureModes.plainTerms: Customer data collected for billing is now training a model. Nobody checked whether customers agreed to that when they handed it over.

failureModes.name: Sensitive data in ungoverned tools
failureModes.plainTerms: Confidential documents are being pasted into tools the company doesn't control, to get a quick summary before a meeting.

failureModes.name: No data-quality gate before use
failureModes.plainTerms: The model started producing strange results. It turns out the input data has been broken for five weeks. Nothing was checking.

failureModes.name: Residency and cross-border rules unenforced
failureModes.plainTerms: Data that is supposed to stay in one country is being processed by a service running somewhere else. Nobody set out to do that; it's just where the vendor's capacity was.

failureModes.name: Retention and deletion not applied to AI artifacts
failureModes.plainTerms: The company deletes customer records after seven years. The prompts and AI outputs containing those same records are kept indefinitely, because nobody classified them as records.

failureModes.name: Conflicting sources of truth
failureModes.plainTerms: Two dashboards show different numbers for the same thing, because they pull from two systems that disagree. Both are being used to make decisions, and nobody knows which one is right.

failureModes.name: No independent validation before first use
failureModes.plainTerms: The team that built the model is the team that checked whether it works.

failureModes.name: Validation not proportionate to materiality
failureModes.plainTerms: A model that sets pricing across the whole business received the same one-page review as a tool that reformats slides.

failureModes.name: System documentation incomplete
failureModes.plainTerms: The documentation is a screenshot and a sentence. Nobody outside the original team could work out what the system actually does.

failureModes.name: No intended-use statement
failureModes.plainTerms: There is no written statement of what the system is for, so when someone asks whether a new use is in scope, there is nothing to compare it against.

failureModes.name: Assumptions and limitations undocumented
failureModes.plainTerms: The model assumes customers behave the way they did three years ago. That assumption is real, load-bearing, and written down nowhere.

failureModes.name: No fairness testing evidence retained
failureModes.plainTerms: Fairness testing was done once, by the team that built it, in a notebook on somebody's laptop. Then the auditor asked for evidence.
failureModes.description: Fairness testing was either not performed or was performed without retaining evidence in a form that satisfies an external auditor. Under several regimes the absence of evidence is itself the violation, independent of whether the system is in fact biased.
failureModes.sectors: Employment screening, lending, insurance underwriting, tenant screening
indicators: No independent audit within the last twelve months on in-scope systems
Testing performed by the building team with no independence
Results held in analyst notebooks rather than in a retained record
No published summary where publication is required
rootCauses: Fairness testing treated as a build-phase activity rather than a recurring obligation
No clear determination of which systems fall in scope of which jurisdiction
Independence requirements misread as satisfied by internal second-line review
mitigations: Commission annual independent audits for in-scope automated employment decision tools
Retain evidence in an audit-ready system of record rather than in analysis artifacts
Maintain an in-scope determination register per jurisdiction
Publish required summaries on schedule

failureModes.reference: Compliance studies since 2023 have repeatedly found low rates of published audit summaries among employers apparently in scope of NYC Local Law 144.

failureModes.name: Generative and agentic systems governed under legacy assumptions
failureModes.plainTerms: A generative assistant is being validated using the checklist written for statistical credit models. The checklist asks for things that don't apply and misses everything that does.
failureModes.description: Generative and agentic systems are either forced into a validation framework designed for deterministic statistical models, or fall into a governance gap because the applicable guidance explicitly excludes them. Both produce controls that do not fit the risk.
failureModes.sectors: Banking most acutely; applicable wherever legacy model risk frameworks exist
indicators: Generative use cases validated using deterministic backtesting methods
No hallucination or groundedness monitoring in place
Agent autonomy levels and tool-access scopes undocumented
Governance guidance predating generative adoption, unrevised
rootCauses: Supervisory guidance expressly places generative and agentic AI out of scope, leaving institutions to self-determine controls with no template
Existing frameworks are the only available machinery, so they are reused by default
Agentic capability changes faster than governance revision cycles
mitigations: Establish a dedicated generative and agentic standard rather than extending the model standard
Implement hallucination, groundedness, and drift monitoring appropriate to non-deterministic output
Maintain an agent registry capturing capability, autonomy level, and tool access
Define validation methods suited to probabilistic systems

mapping.provision: Footnote 3 to § II places generative and agentic AI outside the scope of model risk management, leaving general safety-and-soundness expectations. Institutions must self-determine controls with no supervisory template.

failureModes.reference: A structural gap rather than a discrete incident, created by the 17 Apr 2026 supersession of SR 11-7 and its explicit carve-out.

failureModes.name: No production-readiness gate
failureModes.plainTerms: The idea was reviewed and approved at the concept stage, when it was a slide. It was then built, changed substantially along the way, and went live. Nothing looked at it again before launch.
failureModes.description: Governance reviews the use case at intake but has no second checkpoint before deployment. Because most material design decisions are made after intake, the system that goes live can differ substantially from the one that was assessed — and nothing in the process is positioned to notice.
failureModes.sectors: Cross-sector
indicators: Approval dates consistently preceding build start by a wide margin
No governance event recorded between approval and go-live
Deployed system characteristics differing from the intake record
Production incidents on systems whose governance record shows no issues
No defined criteria for what 'ready to deploy' requires
rootCauses: Governance programme built intake-first, with later lifecycle stages never implemented
Assumption that intake approval covers the whole lifecycle
Deployment owned by delivery teams with no governance touchpoint
No agreed production-readiness criteria to gate against
mitigations: Establish an explicit production-readiness review distinct from intake approval
Define readiness criteria covering monitoring, human oversight, rollback, and documentation
Require confirmation that the deployed system matches the assessed system
Gate deployment access or release approval on the readiness review
Treat material design change during build as a re-assessment trigger

Validation prior to use

failureModes.reference: Commonly identified when a production incident traces back to a system whose governance record appears complete because it was assessed at concept stage.

failureModes.name: No change control over model, prompt or vendor changes
failureModes.plainTerms: Someone changed the prompt driving a customer-facing assistant. It was a two-line edit. There's no record of who, when, or why, and no way to get back to the old one.

failureModes.name: Silent vendor model update
failureModes.plainTerms: The vendor upgraded their model over a weekend. Output quality changed noticeably on Monday. Nobody was told in advance and nothing was re-checked afterwards.

failureModes.name: Change misclassified as non-material
failureModes.plainTerms: 'We just switched models' was logged as a minor configuration change, so it skipped review entirely.

failureModes.name: No rollback plan
failureModes.plainTerms: The new version is behaving badly. There is no agreed, tested way to go back to the old one, so the choice is to leave it running or turn it off.

failureModes.name: Environment drift between test and production
failureModes.plainTerms: It worked in testing. Production has different data, different settings, and different permissions, so it doesn't.

failureModes.name: Governance tooling configuration drift
failureModes.plainTerms: The governance workflow in the test system and the one in the live system aren't the same. Records moved between them quietly lose fields, and items disappear from the queues people actually work from.

failureModes.name: Absent or undocumented drift review
failureModes.plainTerms: The model's accuracy has been sliding for eight months. Nobody looked, because looking wasn't anybody's job.
failureModes.description: Model or system performance is not monitored for degradation over time, or is monitored informally without retained evidence. Performance decays silently until it surfaces as a business failure or an audit finding.
failureModes.sectors: Cross-sector; regulatory consequence highest in banking and biopharma
indicators: No documented drift review within the defined review period
Monitoring dashboards with no owner and no review record
Performance thresholds undefined, so nothing can breach
Alerting configured but routed to an unmonitored channel
rootCauses: Monitoring treated as a technical function detached from governance
No thresholds defined at approval, so there is no baseline to drift from
No named owner and no service level for review
mitigations: Define quantitative performance thresholds at the point of approval
Schedule drift reviews producing retained, dated evidence
Assign a named monitoring owner with a defined service level
Route alerting to a monitored, accountable channel

mapping.provision: Art. 72 — post-market monitoring system, documented and proportionate, running across the system's operational lifetime. The monitoring plan forms part of Annex IV technical documentation. Corrected in v0.3 from Art. 61.
Art. 26(5) — deployers must monitor operation in accordance with instructions for use and inform the provider of risks
MEASURE-2, MANAGE-4 — ongoing measurement and post-deployment management
Clause 9 — performance evaluation
Drift detection and periodic review
Ongoing monitoring

failureModes.reference: Among the most frequently cited technical contributors across AI Incident Database entries involving deployed production systems.

failureModes.name: No performance thresholds defined
failureModes.plainTerms: Everyone agrees performance should be monitored. Nobody has said what 'bad' looks like, so nothing ever triggers and the monitoring is decorative.

failureModes.name: No AI-incident definition or reporting channel
failureModes.plainTerms: Something went wrong with an AI system. Nobody was sure whether it counted as an incident, or who to tell, so it was handled as a bug.

failureModes.name: No feedback loop from incidents into governance
failureModes.plainTerms: The same problem has happened three times. Each time it was fixed. Nothing changed in how things get approved, so it will happen a fourth time.

failureModes.name: No monitoring owner or service level
failureModes.plainTerms: There's a monitoring dashboard. It's genuinely good. No one has opened it since the week it was built.

failureModes.name: Near-misses uncaptured
failureModes.plainTerms: The system nearly caused a serious error and somebody caught it by luck. It was fixed quietly and never written down, so the luck isn't reproducible.

failureModes.name: No stage-aging or cycle-time metric
failureModes.plainTerms: Leadership asks how long approvals are taking. The system can show which stage each item is in, but not how long it's been sitting there — so the real answer is a guess, and it's usually optimistic.

failureModes.name: Evidence gap at audit
failureModes.plainTerms: Every control worked exactly as designed. The auditor asked for proof. The proof was in someone's email, someone else's chat, and a folder nobody could find.
failureModes.description: A control operated correctly but was not documented in a producible form, so compliance cannot be demonstrated at examination or inspection. The organization did the right thing and still receives the finding.
failureModes.sectors: Banking, biopharma, insurance — anywhere external examination occurs
indicators: Evidence assembled reactively in the weeks preceding an examination
Controls described in policy with no corresponding artifact
Evidence scattered across email, chat, and personal drives
Prior findings citing documentation rather than control design
rootCauses: Evidence capture is manual and therefore skipped under operational load
No single system of record, so evidence has no natural home
Controls designed for operation rather than for demonstrability
mitigations: Capture evidence in a system of record at the moment the control operates
Link every control explicitly to its evidence artifact
Collect continuously rather than reactively
Design controls to be demonstrable, not merely effective

failureModes.reference: A common category of finding in model and AI governance examinations, where the deficiency is evidentiary rather than operational.

failureModes.name: No single system of record
failureModes.plainTerms: AI governance records live in a spreadsheet, a ticketing system, three inboxes and a shared drive. There is no single place that is authoritative, so every question has several answers.

failureModes.name: No regulatory mapping maintained
failureModes.plainTerms: The company has controls. Nobody has mapped which control satisfies which regulatory requirement, so every audit starts from zero and takes six weeks.

failureModes.name: Reactive evidence assembly
failureModes.plainTerms: Six weeks before the examination, four people stop their day jobs to reconstruct evidence for the previous two years.

failureModes.name: No periodic re-attestation
failureModes.plainTerms: Systems were approved once. There is no point at which anyone is asked to confirm they're still appropriate, still used as described, or still needed.

failureModes.name: No portfolio-level visibility
failureModes.plainTerms: The board asks how many AI systems the company runs. The honest answer is that nobody knows.
failureModes.description: Governance operates case by case with no aggregated view. Leadership cannot state how many AI systems exist, what their combined risk profile is, or where concentrations sit — so risk is managed locally and never in aggregate.
failureModes.sectors: Cross-sector; consequence rises with portfolio size
indicators: No current count of AI systems in production
Risk reported per use case and never at portfolio level
No catalog of deployed solutions
Board reporting assembled manually each cycle
rootCauses: Governance built for individual approvals rather than portfolio management
Records held across disconnected systems
No aggregate risk methodology defined
mitigations: Maintain a solutions catalog as the authoritative portfolio view
Provide standing executive reporting rather than assembled reporting
Define and apply a portfolio-level risk aggregation method
Track concentration by vendor, model family, and business function

mapping.provision: Aggregate model risk — the 2026 guidance places explicit emphasis on portfolio-level rather than only model-level risk

failureModes.reference: Surfaces as an inability to answer supervisory or board questions rather than as an operational incident.

failureModes.name: Historical attribution lost through organizational change
failureModes.plainTerms: A reorganization moved people between teams. Historical records now show the new structure, so reports about last year's reviews no longer match what actually happened — and the reviewers who did the work have vanished from their own reviews.
failureModes.description: Governance records reflect the current organizational structure rather than the structure in place when the work was performed. Reorganizations, departures, and role changes silently rewrite the historical record, so past reviews can no longer be attributed to the people and functions that actually conducted them.
failureModes.sectors: Cross-sector; severity rises with organizational change frequency and portfolio age
indicators: Historical reports changing values after a reorganization with no underlying record activity
Completed reviews showing reviewers who did not perform them
Departed reviewers disappearing from records they authored
Inability to reproduce a report generated before an organizational change
Reviewer fields that cannot be retired without altering historical records
rootCauses: People and organizational units modelled as live references rather than as values captured at the time
No snapshot taken when an assessment is completed
Removing a person from selection also removes them from history
Record design optimized for current-state operation, not for historical integrity
mitigations: Snapshot completed assessments so historical values are fixed at completion
Distinguish archiving from deletion — retire people from future selection while preserving past attribution
Maintain an active/inactive status distinct from presence in the record
Retain organizational attribution as recorded at the time of the work
Test reproducibility of historical reports as part of any organizational change

mapping.provision: ALCOA+ data integrity — specifically the attributable and enduring principles. An electronic record whose author changes retrospectively fails both, and this is the most direct regulatory anchor for this failure mode.
Audit trail integrity — records must identify who performed an action and must not be obscured by later change
Art. 12 logging; Art. 18 documentation retention
GOVERN-1, MANAGE-4 — documentation and records
Clause 7.5 — documented information, including control of changes
Documentation expectations supporting supervisory review of past decisions

failureModes.reference: Rarely recognized until an examination requires reproducing a report from before a reorganization.

failureModes.name: Governance data model too rigid to record reality
failureModes.plainTerms: The system allows two findings per review. Real reviews routinely produce five. The other three are recorded in a spreadsheet, or not at all — so the official record understates what was actually found.

failureModes.name: Manual bulk remediation of governance records
failureModes.plainTerms: Correcting several hundred governance records has to be done by hand, one at a time, because nothing can safely update them in bulk. Everyone involved knows some of them will end up wrong.

failureModes.name: Findings tracked outside the system of record
failureModes.plainTerms: The review produced eleven action items. They live in a spreadsheet on a shared drive. Whether any of them have been done is anyone's guess.
failureModes.description: Review findings are recorded outside the governance system — typically in spreadsheets, documents, or email threads — so they are disconnected from the use case they concern, invisible in reporting, and dependent on an individual to chase. The review process functions; the remediation process does not exist as a process at all.
failureModes.sectors: Cross-sector; the most common gap between programmes that appear mature and programmes that are
indicators: Action items maintained in spreadsheets or documents rather than in the governance record
No way to report open findings without manual compilation
Status updates obtained by individually contacting owners
Findings with no traceable link to the use case that generated them
Items whose current status nobody can state without asking someone
rootCauses: Governance tooling implemented for intake and review, with remediation never scoped
Findings treated as an output of review rather than as a tracked object
No owner of the remediation process distinct from the review process
Spreadsheet adopted as a stopgap and never replaced
mitigations: Record findings as first-class objects within the governance system of record
Link every finding to its originating review and use case
Generate portfolio-level open-findings reporting as standing output
Automate status requests rather than relying on individual follow-up
Treat the remediation loop as in scope when implementing governance tooling

failureModes.reference: Presents at audit as an inability to demonstrate that identified issues were resolved.

failureModes.name: Findings without owner or due date
failureModes.plainTerms: The finding says 'improve monitoring.' It doesn't say who, or by when, so it belongs to everyone and therefore to no one.

failureModes.name: No escalation on ageing findings
failureModes.plainTerms: An action item has been open for seven months. Nothing happens when it ages. Nobody is notified, and it appears on no report.

failureModes.name: Findings closed without evidence
failureModes.plainTerms: The owner marked the item complete. There's no attachment, no link, and no description of what they actually did — just a status that changed.

failureModes.name: No blocked or on-hold status
failureModes.plainTerms: The item is stuck waiting on somebody else, but the only available statuses are open and closed. So it looks like the owner is sitting on it, and the metrics blame the wrong person.

failureModes.name: Findings not linked to the use case record
failureModes.plainTerms: The finding exists. The use case it came from exists. Nothing connects them, so anyone reviewing that use case later sees a clean record.

failureModes.name: No aggregate view of open findings
failureModes.plainTerms: Nobody can answer how many open findings exist across the AI portfolio, how old they are, or which are overdue — so remediation is never discussed at the level where it could be resourced.
